en: The Sūtra on the Merit of Offering Lamps Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas of India during the Northern Qi Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra, saying: “Śāriputra!

The Buddha possesses four kinds of supreme, wondrous, and virtuous dharmas, which enable sentient beings to attain immeasurable fruits, immeasurable radiance, immeasurable exquisite forms, immeasurable treasuries of merit, immeasurable treasuries of bliss, and immeasurable treasuries of precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, the knowledge and vision of liberation, and eloquence—all of which are unattached and untainted dharmas.”
“Śāriputra! What are the four?
First, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has attained the śīlapāramitā and is endowed with immeasurable precepts;”
Second, they attain the dhyāna-pāramitā, being endowed with immeasurable concentrations;

third, they attain the prajñā-pāramitā, being endowed with immeasurable wisdom, vast wisdom, penetrative wisdom, wisdom according to the nature of reality, innumerable wisdom, decisive wisdom, and definitive knowledge and vision;
fourth, they attain an unturbid mind and a mind of excellent mastery, being endowed with wondrous liberation and supreme liberation.
These are the four kinds of supreme, wondrous, and wholesome dharmas.
"Śāriputra, this Buddha,
Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has completely distanced himself from all evils."
All wholesome dharmas are fully accomplished; all practices are complete; they possess the vision of reality as it is;
they are far removed from darkness and are able to radiate light; they are endowed with immeasurable provisions of merit and wisdom;
they outshine the world and cannot be eclipsed by the world; and they have attained morality, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Liberation, the knowledge and vision of liberation, the perfection of the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses,
the attainment of all the Buddha-dharmas and powers, the ability to fully possess the powers of all Buddhas,
the attainment of the great compassion and eloquence of all Buddhas, and the fulfillment of original vows and skillful means— having well cultivated these roots...
Possessing the jewel of wisdom, his diligence is immeasurable and never ceases;
he is free from all sorrow and grief, without affliction or attachment, and is well-subdued.
As a great dragon king, he is devoid of residual habits and serves as the unsurpassed field of merit for all sentient beings.

“Śāriputra! If bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, having generated a pure mind, for the sake of seeking merit and out of love for merit, contemplate the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed skillful means and the fulfillment of his original practices throughout all births and deaths until the end of the future; and in the present life, achieve immeasurable, unattached morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—even contemplating a single quality of mindfulness of the Buddha;”

Having recollected these merits, throughout immeasurable billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of kalpas, because they have cultivated roots of goodness in the fields of the three knowledges (*trividyā*), in the field of pure precepts, in the field of unequaled precepts, and in the field of immeasurable true merit—whether before stūpas or various images—they have established offerings by presenting lamps. Even with a small wick, or by anointing it with ghee or oil and lighting it, they have offered it so that its light illuminates but a single step of the path.
“Śāriputra! Such merit cannot be fully understood by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; only a Buddha, a Tathāgata, is able to know it!”
Śāriputra!

If even those who seek worldly rewards produce such merit and virtue, how much more so for those sons and daughters of good family who, with a pure heart of deep joy, without seeking any karmic fruit, dwell in reverent mindfulness of the Buddha’s merits in an uninterrupted succession? The merit produced by such individuals is truly immeasurable.
Śāriputra!

If the merit of illuminating even a single step of the path is already such, how much more so for illuminating an entire flight of steps—the path of two steps, three steps, or four steps; or reaching one tier, two tiers, or even many tiers of the stupa body;
or one side, two sides, up to all four sides, as well as the image of the Buddha?
“Śāriputra! That lamp which was lit may sometimes go out quickly; it may be extinguished by the wind, or by the exhaustion of the oil, or by the exhaustion of the wick, or by the exhaustion of both.”
For example, when dragons, out of anger, produce clouds that hang low and give rise to lightning within them, which vanishes as soon as it appears. "Śāriputra!

In the same way, if a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śrāmaṇera, śrāmaṇerikā, upāsaka, or upāsikā—or even another person who has not received the precepts—offers a small lamp at a stūpa or temple for the sake of delighting in the good, for the sake of protecting their own person, and out of faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, the fruit of retribution and the mass of merit obtained from offering such a small lamp to the Field of Merit can only be known by the Buddha. It cannot be known by any in the world—gods, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas—not even by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas."
The meritorious retribution received from lighting such a small lamp cannot be described in words.
"Śāriputra! The realm of the Buddhas is inconceivable; only a Tathāgata knows this meaning."
Śāriputra! The mass of merit obtained by that person who gives lamps is immeasurable and boundless, beyond calculation; only a Tathāgata is able to fully know it.
Śāriputra!

If the merit of even a small lamp-lighting is thus incalculable, how much more so for those who, after my parinirvāṇa, at a Buddha-stūpa or monastery, either perform the act themselves or instruct others to do so—whether lighting one lamp, two lamps, or even many lamps; or offering incense, flowers, garlands, precious banners, streamers, canopies, and various other kinds of excellent and sublime offerings?
“Śāriputra, there are four kinds of dharmas that should be accepted with faith.
What are these four?
First, you should have faith and acceptance that the Buddha-dharma is immeasurable;
second, you should have faith and acceptance that by cultivating even a small root of goodness, one obtains immeasurable retribution;

third, regarding the merit and retribution obtained from generating deep reverence and faith in the Triple Gem and properly practicing wholesome deeds—even you Śrāvakas who now see me face to face cannot fully know it, nor can you conceive of or fathom it—how much less could my Śrāvaka disciples who live far away after my parinirvāṇa possibly know it directly or fathom it?
If there were anyone capable of knowing or fathoming this, it would be impossible; one should therefore accept it with faith.
Fourth, these śrāvakas are unable to know or measure all the actions performed by sentient beings, nor the karmic retributions resulting from those actions.
Śāriputra! You śrāvakas need not deliberate upon this matter. Why is that?
Śāriputra! The Tathāgata has always taught that the karmic actions and their retributions of all sentient beings are inconceivable;
the Buddhas of the past, the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas, have likewise already declared that the karmic retribution of sentient beings is inconceivable.
The future Buddhas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas shall likewise declare that the karmic retribution of sentient beings is inconceivable.
The faith of sentient beings' minds and the intrinsic nature of their minds are likewise unknowable and inconceivable; this meaning should be accepted with faith!

“Śāriputra! You disciples who abide in the noble lineages possess no true eye nor skillful means regarding the karmic retributions of all sentient beings; how much less so for others whose minds are light, thin, feeble, and inferior—those who are devoid of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; those who have lost right mindfulness; those shrouded in the darkness of ignorance with eyes heavily veiled—who are unable to know the various phenomena within and without their own bodies: ‘Who, ultimately, am I?’”
Who am I? Where do I dwell?
Are my merits great or small?
"How shall I act so as to be in accordance with the precepts, or how shall I act so as not to be in accordance with the precepts?
Am I one who maintains right mindfulness regarding the precepts, or am I one who has lost mindfulness regarding the precepts?
Is the action I perform the action of a wise person, or is it the action of a fool?"
"From where do they come, and to where do they go? Śāriputra!
Even ordinary worldlings with inverted views do not know such matters regarding their own bodies; how much less could they know the various karmic retributions of all sentient beings?"
If one could know [this], it would be impossible. "Śāriputra, for the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha,

there is no decrease in morality, no decrease in concentration, no decrease in wisdom, no decrease in liberation, no decrease in the knowledge and vision of liberation, and no decrease in his physical marks."

Śāriputra! The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha possesses immeasurable precepts, unimpeded precepts, inconceivable precepts, incomparable precepts, ultimate precepts, and pure precepts; that Tathāgata knows, exactly as they are, all the karma and the karmic retributions of all sentient beings.
“Śāriputra, how does the Tathāgata know the karmic retribution of all sentient beings as it truly is?
Śāriputra, [it is thus:]”
The Buddha knows thus:
there are sentient beings whose wholesome karma is exhausted while unwholesome karma increases;
and there are sentient beings whose unwholesome karma is exhausted while wholesome karma increases.
There are some sentient beings for whom wholesome karma is about to arise and unwholesome karma is about to perish;
there are other sentient beings for whom unwholesome karma is about to arise and wholesome karma is about to perish. Śāriputra!

In this way, the Tathāgata enters into the various distinctions among the karma and karmic retributions of all sentient beings, knowing them all as they truly are: that certain sentient beings may be ignorant or deluded, while others may be virtuous or unvirtuous.
Śāriputra! I possess such wisdom and such skillful means that I am able to explain and prophesy all the inconceivable and various karmic retributions of sentient beings.
“Śāriputra! If there are sentient beings who have perfected faith, they are able to believe in me.

Furthermore, if there are sentient beings who lack faith, who distance themselves from my Dharma, do not believe my words, and slander me, they will, for a long night, find neither meaning nor benefit, but will fall into suffering and affliction.”

Śāriputra! If those sentient beings offer lamps as a gift to the Buddha’s stūpas and shrines, by virtue of the wholesome karma created through this offering, they will be able to obtain the fruit of peace, happiness, and delight.
When that person performs the wholesome deed of giving a lamp-light offering, they do so with joy and arising from faith; in the present life, they attain three kinds of pure minds.
What are these three?
Those sons and daughters of good family form this thought:
"I have already made offerings to the Tathāgata; knowing that the body is not solid, I maintain the perception of a solid body;
knowing the faults of wealth, I maintain the perception of solid wealth."
"Śāriputra! This is called the first pure mind for making offerings to a Buddha stūpa.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
Those sons and daughters of good family give rise to this thought:
"I have already made offerings to the Tathāgata, the unsurpassed field of merit, the most supreme field of merit, who is capable of receiving the most supreme offerings."
I now have no fear of falling into the realms of hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts.

These roots of goodness of mine have already become the causes for rebirth in the wholesome paths of humans and devas; they will secure exquisite physical forms and all necessities of life, as well as wisdom, peace, and happiness, even unto the attainment of the fruit of Bodhi.
"Śāriputra! This is called the second pure mind for making offerings to a Buddha stūpa.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
Those sons and daughters of good family form this thought:
"I have already performed acts of giving to the Buddhas; I have already cultivated merit; I have already abandoned stinginess and greed; I have already eliminated the fault of avarice."
Having formed this thought, his mind of giving becomes free from stinginess, and his mind of giving increases. Śāriputra,
this is called the third pure mind of making offerings to a Buddha stūpa.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
if a son of good family or a daughter of good family has offered a lamp before a Buddha stūpa or temple, they will attain three kinds of illumination at the time of their death."
What are the three?

First, when those sons or daughters of good family approach the end of their lives, all the merit they have previously cultivated will manifest before them, and they will mindfully recollect wholesome dharmas without forgetting them.
Śāriputra! This is the first clarity;
by means of this, one is able to recollect and know that one has previously planted various roots of goodness under the Buddha.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
at the time of their death, those good men and good women will attain such a recollection:
"I have already made offerings before the images of the Buddha, stupas, temples, and so forth."
Having formed this thought, his heart was filled with exultation.
Śāriputra, these are the two types of clear knowledge;
Therefore, they are able to give rise to the mindfulness of the Buddha.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, when those good men and good women are at the point of death, they see other sentient beings practicing generosity; having seen others do so, they give rise to this thought:
"I too once offered lamps at the stūpas of the Buddhas; I shall now likewise practice giving!
By reflecting upon giving, one attains a joyful mind;
having attained a joyful mind, there is no suffering of death.
Śāriputra! These are the three knowledges;
by means of them, one attains the mind that recollects the Dharma.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a son or daughter of good family offers lamps as an act of giving within a Buddha stūpa or temple, at the time of their death, they shall again behold four kinds of light."
What are the four?
First, at the time of death, one sees the full orb of the sun rising;
second, one sees the full orb of the pure moon rising.
Third, he saw the hosts of devas seated together in one place;

fourth, he saw the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha sitting at the Bodhi tree on the verge of attaining enlightenment, and seeing himself there as well, he paid homage to the Tathāgata with his ten fingers joined in palms-pressed salutation and remained there in reverent devotion.
“Śāriputra!
This is called the attainment of these four kinds of light at the time of death after having offered lamps at the stūpas and shrines of the Buddha.
When the World-Honored One had finished explaining this meaning, he further spoke in verse:
“If a person makes offerings to the stupas and temples of the Unsurpassed Dharma King, the Great Seer,
that wise one, having performed this deed, shall obtain boundless and supreme bliss.”

At the time of death, one does not lose mindfulness; Being able to see the lamps one offered in the past, One attains four kinds of joy and is freed from all transgressions, Remaining undeluded and unconfused at the moment of passing.
At the moment of death, one sees the radiance of the ten directions;
One beholds the sun and moon rising from the earth, And sees thousands of millions of nayutas of devas, To whom one preaches the Buddha-dharma for the sake of those celestial hosts.
His parents, wife, children, and kinsmen all surround him, wailing with great compassion;
yet the deceased neither thinks of them nor looks upon them, for that person’s right mindfulness remains ever undisturbed.
Now one beholds the celestial palaces before them, And with a mind at peace in the presence of the goddesses;
Furthermore, one sees the various adorned gardens, Within which the supreme five desires are fully present.
Again, I see the Buddha seated beneath the Bodhi tree, surrounded by devas, humans, and asuras;
I see myself standing before the Buddha with palms joined, making offerings to the Supreme Muni.
Having seen the Teacher, they revered him deeply; with hearts full of joy, they entreated the Tathāgata.
Seeing their joyful hearts, the World-Honored One did not refuse their request, but accepted it.
This person’s aspirations are fulfilled and joy pervades them; at the time of passing away, they experience no suffering or distress.
Having found delight in the Buddha, they shall have no great fear at the hour of death.
At the time of death, one does not lose mindfulness;
One beholds the ten directions, all brilliantly illuminated, And sees unprecedented, most wondrous forms— This is the karmic fruit of offering lamps.
After death, one will certainly be reborn in the heavens;
seeing oneself seated upon a celestial couch, surrounded by heavenly maidens—this fruit is obtained because of making offerings to the Buddha.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
having offered lamps at the stupas and temples of the Buddha, one will be reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three after death;
having been born in that heaven, one attains purity in five matters."
Śāriputra! How do those devas attain purity in five matters?
First, they attain a pure body;...
Second, they shall attain preeminent majesty and virtue among the devas;
third, they shall constantly possess pure mindfulness and wisdom;
fourth, they shall constantly hear sounds that accord with their wishes.
Fifth, the retinues they obtain always act in accordance with their wishes, so that their hearts are filled with joy. Śāriputra,
these are called the five matters in which those devas attain purity.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“That deva attained a body of radiant light, Endowed with merit and honored by others;
He became the leader of a thousand sons of gods, Because he offered lamps at the stūpa of the Buddha.”
The celestial sounds one hears are always pleasing to the mind; their sorrowful beauty is exquisite and surpasses that of other devas.
Endowed with the foremost and supreme mindfulness and wisdom, one further attains the most excellent and superior retinue.
Wherever that deva-son goes, all the gods look up to him with reverence;
what kind of karma did he practice in the past, that he has now attained such a radiant body?
There are trees all named "Supreme Joy," their surrounding radiance like that of the moon;
those gods have obtained these wondrous trees and use them to adorn the celestial palaces and gardens.
Immeasurable devas were all struck with wonder: "What is the name of this tree’s flower?
Like the brilliant radiance of a lamp, it universally emits wondrous and exquisite incense."
All the retinues belonging to that deva adorn their bodies with the flowers of those trees;
amidst immeasurable billions of devas, their radiance shines forth like the sun.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Having offered lamps at the stūpas and shrines of the Buddha, one is reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
Once born there, that deity knows of itself: 'At such a time, I dwell here;'"
"At such a time, I shall pass away.
When that eminent son of heaven was about to die, he preached the Dharma and exhorted his retinue and the other celestial hosts, causing them to rejoice.

Having relinquished their lifespan in those celestial palaces, they do not fall into the evil realms, but are born into the most noble lineages among humans, into families that have faith in the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, even if there is no Buddha in the world, they are likewise never born into families that recklessly pursue omens of fortune and misfortune or hold false views.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“That deva has attained such wisdom, Knowing how long he shall dwell among the devas;
That deva is likewise able to know for himself: ‘Before long, my life shall now come to an end.’”
When the five signs of death appear, and that deva’s lifespan is about to end,
he immediately preaches the Dharma for billions of devas, remaining free from delusion and without sorrow in his heart.
Among the assembly of devas, he spoke these words:
"All conditioned things are impermanent and devoid of pleasure; some are born and some die.
One should not fail to contemplate death while preaching this Dharma."
All those kinsmen were filled with grief and distress, and the same was true for the immeasurable hosts of devas;
yet although he himself beheld the five signs, he did not grieve, reflecting instead upon his own merits.
When his life in that celestial palace has ended, he immediately descends to be born among humans;
dwelling in the womb and emerging from it, his mindfulness remains undisturbed, and he constantly experiences bliss without any suffering or affliction.
Having been born, he immediately attains the supernormal power of recollecting past lives, And is able to remember his original place of origin;
Recalling the suffering within the human realm, he does not crave its pleasures, For death arrives in an instant, pressing him with urgency.
Having reflected upon the retribution within the heavens, one finds no true joy even in this human realm;
if even the heavens are suffering, how much more so the human world?
All conditioned existences are insubstantial and constantly shifting.
Once that person has reached maturity, they will surely renounce the household life to become a monastic;
with a mind that never engages in unwholesome thoughts or reflections, they shall obtain such a fruit:
in every successive birth they will constantly attain the supernormal power of recollecting past lives, and they will also never again commit any unwholesome deeds.
He will certainly leave the household life and uphold the pure precepts;
this is the fruit of his offering of lamp-light.
He shall never be blind or crippled, and his eyes shall never be obscured at any time.
The body shall be free from illness and ill repute; the mind shall always be sharp and wise, never dull or deluded.
Furthermore, one shall forever be free from eye ailments;
wherever one is born, the eyes shall not be squinting, nor shall one be one-eyed or blind, and those eyes shall always be clear and undisturbed.
The eyes are long and well-proportioned, with black and white clearly distinguished, Like the pure and exquisite petals of a blue lotus;
The eyes are so clear they can see even the most minute objects, Just like a transparent and luminous mani jewel.
Throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, they obtain pure fleshly eyes that never fail or decay;
they also remain forever free from all eye diseases—this is the fruit of offering lamps.
Well-sealed by roots of goodness and skilled in all treatises, thoroughly mastering every craft and art;
that wise person, through skillful observation, possesses wondrous wisdom capable of perceiving the ultimate truth.
Skillfully observing that all states of existence lack self-mastery, one attains illumination within the Buddha-dharma;
seeing all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, one pays them reverence and practices offerings upon having seen them.
In every birth one attains a most excellent and upright appearance; relatives and kinsmen all respect and love them;
they obtain great wealth and jewels with sovereign power, as well as an indestructible circle of followers.
Just as the light of a lamp can dispel darkness, blazing and illuminating all directions, so too is the radiance of that person; it cannot be obscured by the gloom of darkness.
If one gives rise to faith in a Buddha stūpa, Offering excellent lamps, garlands, and necklaces—
When giving these lamps with a pure mind, One attains the state of the most supreme among men.
Of upright and exquisite beauty, most lovely, Delightful to all the world,
yet his mind does not lightly grasp at good or ill fortune, Nor does he take pleasure in the heterodox paths of the world.
All the evil views existing in the world, as well as heterodox paths and the like, he does not accept;
if he is a king, he is always content and does not covet other lands to incite war or strife.
Always free from suffering and affliction, and likewise without grief;
Furthermore, they are without the fever of distress, and possess no decline whatsoever; Moreover, they have no ill repute and no decay or torment.
If one speaks as a minister to a king, neither the king nor the people will fail to believe them;
their body shall never suffer from emaciation or disease, and they shall not become a eunuch or engage in unrighteous conduct.
Endowed with perfect physical marks, they dwell in peace and happiness;
afflictions and suffering cannot touch their bodies, nor do they see any evil dreams; whether sleeping or awake, they are always tranquil and secure.
Life after life they shall be able to obtain all hidden treasures and make offerings to the caityas of all Buddhas;
as the virtues of the Buddhas are boundless, so too shall be what those people attain.
“Śāriputra! If there are sentient beings who offer lamps at the stupas and shrines of the Buddha, they shall obtain four kinds of delightful dharmas.
What are these four?
First, the physical body;
second, material wealth;
third, great goodness.
Fourth is wisdom. Śāriputra,
if there are sentient beings who offer lamps at the stūpas of the Buddha, they shall attain such delightful dharmas as these.
At that time, the Tathāgata, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke again in verse:
"With a body well-proportioned and endowed with great strength, Not engaging in battle or strife with others,
Wandering through all directions without causing distress— This is due to having offered lamps at the stūpas of the Buddha."
Born into a family of great wealth and noble lineage, Endowed with merit and revered by all people,
May they always attain the knowledge of past lives in every birth, By virtue of having offered lamps to the stūpas of the Buddha.
Always mindful with compassion for all sentient beings, The words they utter are respectfully received by their kin;
Their minds are free from malice and ever-gentle, Never performing deeds that lead to the evil realms.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
if there are sentient beings who make offerings to a Buddha-stūpa, they will attain four kinds of purity. What are these four?
First, purity of physical action;
second, purity of verbal action;
third, purity of mental action.
Fourth is the purity of virtuous friends. "Śāriputra,
how does one attain purity of bodily action?"

If a son or daughter of good family, in whatever place of birth they may be, abstains from taking life and harbors no intent to harm, and likewise always abstains from stealing and sexual misconduct—refraining even from improper conduct with their own wife, let alone with the wives of others.

Furthermore, they do not drink alcohol or indulge in heedless self-indulgence; they do not oppress sentient beings with swords, staves, or other instruments of suffering, and they remain free from unwholesome states and all evil deeds.
“Śāriputra! To remain far removed from these things is called purity of bodily action. Śāriputra!”
What is purity of verbal karma?

Such a person, throughout successive lifetimes, never speaks falsely; if they have not seen or heard something, they never speak of it falsely. If they have seen or heard it, they wait for the appropriate time to inquire, and only then do they speak. For the benefit of themselves and others, they do not make contradictory statements.

Even if someone were to command them to speak falsely, they would never utter a lie for the sake of protecting truthful speech; they would not repeat what was said to one person to another, nor would they report what happened to one person to another.
He prevents the two factions from first becoming estranged and does not allow them to increase; whatever he speaks is able to skillfully reconcile disputes.

He completely distances himself from words that cause pain, harsh words, bitter and evil words, unpleasant words, disagreeable words, unlovely words, words that do not enter the heart, words that afflict others, and words that bind one in enmity.

Whatever words they utter are moist, gentle, well-intentioned, non-coarse, pleasing to the ear, beautiful, heart-penetrating, beloved by many, delightful to many, lovely, charming, and capable of dispelling enmity; they always speak such various kinds of exquisite and beautiful words.

Furthermore, he abstains from frivolous speech; he does not harbor divergent thoughts while speaking divergently, nor does he employ divergent gestures or divergent agreements to conceal the truth. He does not engage in tedious prolixity, does not speak at improper times, and always speaks with ultimate clarity.
Śāriputra! In this way, one distances oneself from impure verbal karma and accomplishes pure verbal karma. Śāriputra!
This is called purity of verbal action.
"Śāriputra, what is purity of mental action?"

Regarding all the precious treasures and wealth belonging to others, they do not give rise to greedy attachment, do not give rise to anger, remain far removed from harmful intent, and further abandon wrong views, being free from all evil perspectives.
Śāriputra! To remain far removed from these things is called purity of mental action. Śāriputra!
How does one attain purity of spiritual friends?

If there are spiritual friends who are far removed from false speech, do not drink intoxicants, are free from all coarseness and violence, and have subdued themselves with right view—one should go to them, attend upon them, and consult them for instruction.

Furthermore, he approaches the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and others, attending upon and making offerings to them, and inquires about and receives teachings not yet heard. Śāriputra,
this is called the fourth purity of a spiritual friend.
“Śāriputra! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family offers a lamp before a stūpa of the Buddha, they shall obtain these four kinds of purity.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"To light a lamp for the purpose of illuminating the stūpa, To have well-subdued the actions of body, speech, and mind,
To be far removed from false views and endowed with pure precepts— By means of these, one obtains the eye of intentionality."
Just as the pure sun shines upon the ten directions, he swiftly attains the exhaustion of outflows;
possessing great wisdom and majestic power, he gains the pure divine eye, free from dust and taints.
The wise are able to understand the intentions of sentient beings, And they also attain supernormal powers, clarity, and eloquence;
It is not difficult for them to seek and attain the paths of the two vehicles, For by offering lamps to the Buddha, they obtain such rewards.
If one seeks unsurpassed Buddha-enlightenment, divine vision, wisdom, and material wealth—
these three things will never diminish, by virtue of offering lamps at the stūpas of the Buddha.

“Śāriputra! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family abides in the Mahāyāna and offers lamps at the stūpas and shrines of the Buddha, they will obtain eight kinds of delightful and superior dharmas in every lifetime.”
What are the eight?
First, obtaining the superior fleshly eye;
second, attaining superior mindfulness that cannot be measured by others.
Third, they attain the supreme, transcendent divine eye;
fourth, for the sake of fulfilling the cultivation and accumulation of the Path, they attain unimpaired precepts;
fifth, they attain the fulfillment of wisdom and realize nirvana.
Sixth, through previously performed wholesome deeds, one attains a state free from obstacles;
seventh, through the wholesome karma performed, one encounters the Buddhas and is able to serve as the eye for all sentient beings;

eighth, if a son or daughter of good family, by means of those roots of goodness, becomes a wheel-turning monarch, the precious wheel he obtains will not be obstructed by others, and his body will be upright and handsome.
Sometimes he becomes Śakra, attaining great majestic power and being endowed with a thousand eyes;
sometimes he becomes Brahmā, skillfully knowing the affairs of Brahmā and attaining great meditative concentration.
Śāriputra! By means of those roots of goodness dedicated toward enlightenment, one attains these eight kinds of delightful and superior dharmas.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Furthermore, sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Mahāyāna attain eight kinds of immeasurable, supreme dharmas:
first, they attain the immeasurable Buddha-eye;
second, they attain the immeasurable supernormal powers of the Tathāgatas.
Third, they attain the immeasurable precepts of the Buddhas;
fourth, they attain the immeasurable samādhis of the Tathāgatas;
fifth, they attain the immeasurable wisdom of the Tathāgatas.
Sixth, they attain the liberation of the immeasurable Tathāgatas;
seventh, they attain the Buddha’s immeasurable knowledge and vision of liberation;
eighth, they attain entry into the hearts and inclinations of all sentient beings.
Śāriputra! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family offers lamps to the stupas and temples of the Buddha, they will be able to gather such immeasurable and supreme rewards.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If there are sentient beings who, upon seeing one who preaches the Dharma, form this thought:
"How can I cause them to always proclaim and reveal the Buddha-dharma?
I shall offer lamps to them."
"By giving an oil lamp, may the teacher of the Dharma obtain the gift of the lamp of Dharma.
Having formed this thought, he offered the lamp. Through the roots of goodness from this gift of light, he attained eight kinds of immeasurable provisions.
What are these eight?
First, attaining the immeasurable provisions for right mindfulness;
second, attaining the immeasurable provisions for great wisdom.
Third, they attain the immeasurable provisions of faith;
fourth, they attain the immeasurable provisions of diligence;
fifth, they attain the immeasurable provisions of great wisdom.
Sixth, they attain the immeasurable provisions for samādhi;
seventh, they attain the immeasurable provisions for eloquence;
eighth, they attain the immeasurable provisions for merit.

Śāriputra! These are called the eight kinds of requisites for offering lamps; by means of them, one also attains the four unhindered analytical knowledges, and proceeds step by step until the attainment of all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if there are good men or good women who,

in the presence of the Tathāgata, see another person offering a lamp, and with pure faith join their ten fingers in palms-together gesture and give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy, they shall, through these roots of goodness, attain eight kinds of superior qualities."
What are the eight?
First, attaining superior physical appearance;
second, attaining superior retinues;
Third, they attain superior ethical discipline;
fourth, they attain superior rebirth among humans and devas;
fifth, they attain superior faith.
Sixth, they attain superior eloquence;
seventh, they attain the superior noble path;
eighth, they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Śāriputra! These are called the eight kinds of superior dharmas. Śāriputra!
For what reason can one obtain these eight kinds of superior and victorious dharmas?

Śāriputra, because the Buddha possesses immeasurable morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, those who make offerings to him likewise obtain immeasurable karmic fruits and benefits.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Having undertaken the practice of renunciation, Diligently cultivating the Buddha-dharma,
One casts off the host of death As an elephant crushes a grove of flowers."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Śāriputra:
"There are five things most difficult to obtain:
first, obtaining a human body is difficult."
Second, it is difficult to attain faith and joy in the Buddha’s true Dharma;
third, it is difficult to take delight in the Buddha’s Dharma and leave the household life;
fourth, it is difficult to be endowed with pure precepts.
Fifth is the difficulty of attaining the exhaustion of outflows. Śāriputra!
For all sentient beings, these five things are the most difficult to obtain; you have already attained them.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate the preceding meaning and to exhort Śāriputra and the others, spoke these verses:
“The Tathāgata’s caityas practice giving, Seeking bodhi for the benefit of sentient beings;
The wise create this supreme cause, And in birth after birth always obtain the most excellent reward.”
Receiving superior births among devas and humans, he is honored with offerings by gods and men alike;
like Mount Sumeru, he remains steadfast and unmoving, his radiance universally illuminating the ten directions.
The hosts of devas see him and all pay him respect; they likewise cherish him and give rise to faith.
They present offerings and offer praise; all rejoice as they behold him again and again.

How marvelous is this celestial mark of merit! Like the light of Brahmā illuminating the Brahma-palace, what karma did this deity perform in the past, that the radiance of his body’s brilliance has become such as this?
Who is seen not to cultivate goodness?
Who does not practice the noble lineage of precepts?
Who, upon seeing the Muni, gives rise to a heart of weary detachment?
Who, having heard the sublime Dharma, would be heedless?
In former times, while dwelling among humans, they constantly offered lamps at the stūpas of the Tathāgata;
having once made offerings within the Buddha-dharma, they well obtained merit and were born in the heavens.
May I always obtain a human body, And give rise to pure faith within the Buddha’s Dharma;
May I never be negligent, abiding in the path of the Buddha, Willingly sacrificing my life rather than abandoning the Dharma.
To obtain a human body is most difficult; why, then, do fools not perform meritorious deeds?
They squander their wealth and resources without practicing the Dharma, and once dead, they fall straight into a great abyss.
Having seen the stainless majesty and virtue, the deva felt remorse in his heart and made this vow:
"May I always be born among humans and diligently practice the holy life;
may I, at the time of my final death, attain pure faith within the Buddha-dharma."
May I attain right mindfulness without forgetfulness, And behold immeasurable Tathāgatas.
May I be honored by a thousand billion devas, And enjoy the company of celestial maidens;
May all the hosts of celestial maidens revere and love me, As they adorn themselves and sport in the gardens.
The celestial fragrances from all directions come to perfume him; his ears hear every kind of wondrous sound.
Wherever this deity travels, he constantly beholds the most sublime forms.

All forms that may be seen are lovely; they never behold any unpleasant sights, and they also constantly obtain superior and exquisite tactile sensations—all this is due to offering lamps at a caitya.

Having passed away from there, he is born into the human realm; Maintaining right mindfulness while dwelling in the womb of his parents, Once born, he remembers the events of that celestial realm, And through the power of wisdom, he does not lose them.
That person, having performed such deeds, Became a wheel-turning king of great power;
The king’s physical form was exceedingly sublime— Such is the retribution obtained by offering lamps.
By virtue of that karma, he obtained a long life;
A vessel of perpetual purity, peace, and bliss, His body free from all ailments and pain— Such was the fruit obtained by Dīpaṃkara.
There shall be no calamity from kings, nor danger from hostile thieves;
others will not dare to violate their wives, nor will they be troubled by wicked people, because they offered lamps as an offering to the Buddha.
Secure, abundant, and free from fear, Magnificent, sovereign, and rich in treasures,
Obtaining exquisite necklaces and gardens— All this results from offering lamps to the Buddha.
When he beholds the Buddha, the World-Honored One, Upon seeing him, his heart gives rise to reverence and faith;
With a joyful mind, he makes offerings to the Buddha, And relinquishing the royal throne, he goes forth into homelessness.
The Buddha possesses immeasurable wisdom and ultimate wisdom; endowed with praiseworthy virtues, he is able to transform others.
Having offered a lamp at this Buddha-stūpa, that person’s bodily radiance shall shine like a lamp.
The Muni, the Bull among Men, with his pure eyes, Illuminated that stupa with excellent lamps;
Having attained the untainted, unsurpassed path, The radiance of his body shines throughout the ten directions.

Having seen the Four Noble Truths and perfected the Ten Powers, And having also brought the Unshared Qualities to completion, He attained the all-seeing eye and became a Sugata; All these fruits arise from the gift of lamps.
Even if all sentient beings had in the past made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas,
possessed great majestic power, perceived the true meaning, and attained the path of a Pratyekabuddha over the course of billions of kalpas.
In all worlds throughout the ten directions, One might arrange lamps and garlands without exception;
If someone with a faithful heart were to offer All those lamps and garlands from every world.
If such a person were to practice such offerings, continuing them without interruption for immeasurable eons,
yet another person were to offer a single lamp to the Buddha, the merit they would obtain would exceed the former by an immeasurable amount.
The lamp oil is like the waters of the great ocean, and its wick is like Mount Sumeru;
if there were someone able to light such a lamp, it would illuminate all worlds everywhere.
This person, with a deep heart of reverence and faith, sets their will solely upon seeking the path of the pratyekabuddha;
they place such lamps throughout the ten directions, honoring and making offerings to them with a single-minded devotion.

If a person generates the mind of enlightenment and holds a grass torch in their hand to offer it briefly to the Buddha, that person will obtain merit exceeding the former; I speak thus because I perceive the true meaning.
All sentient beings throughout the ten directions, each providing offerings as described above,
for immeasurable kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, with minds seeking only the path of the pratyekabuddha.
If there is someone who, at a Buddha’s stupa or temple, lights a single lamp or performs a single prostration,
seeking the unsurpassed path for the sake of sentient beings, this merit exceeds the former and is immeasurable.
The realm of the Buddha is difficult to see and difficult to conceive;
the wise who hear it immediately give rise to joy, while those without faith find no pleasure in hearing it—those foolish Māras destroy the True Dharma.
To realize the pure Dharma-realm is exceedingly difficult; the Sugata alone is such throughout all worlds.
Therefore, you all should rejoice and aspire to seek the virtues of the Buddha.

When the World-Honored One had finished preaching this Dharma, the Venerable Śāriputra and others—immeasurable devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and other beings, both human and non-human—hearing what the Buddha had spoken, all resolved to attain unexcelled bodhicitta. Rejoicing immeasurably, they paid their respects and departed.
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Merit of Offering Lamps.
